spring.title: Spring at Kingfisher Hollow
spring.intro: Spring begins with rain and thaw in the low places. Woodland flowers make the most of the light before the trees leaf out, and frogs and insects become part of life around the warming water.
spring.next_observation: Choose a patch of woodland you can photograph from the same spot every week. Include the canopy and forest floor in the frame, and record whether any plants are in bud, in flower, or leafing out.

passages.title: After the rain
passages.body: Rain and thaw fill shallow pools in the woods. In New York, spotted salamanders leave their winter shelters on mild, rainy nights and move to these pools to lay eggs.
passages.look_for: From a dry bank, look for amphibian egg masses and photograph them in place. Record whether you saw eggs, a moving animal, or heard a call.

claims.text: Spotted salamander eggs mark that early-spring transition at the Hollow.

passages.title: Under the open canopy
passages.body: Spring wildflowers brighten the forest floor while the branches are still bare. Trout lilies make use of that brief window of sunlight, followed in May by white starflower blooms as shade deepens.
passages.look_for: Photograph the leaf pattern and include a flower or bud when you can see one on the same plant.

passages.title: Life at the water's edge
passages.body: By late spring, the canopy shades the woodland floor while the pond still catches the sun. Gray treefrogs can call from branches near breeding water, and adult dragonflies hunt along sunny water margins.
passages.look_for: Save a short recording if you hear a frog. Note the time, and keep the recording linked to the same date as any photographs.

rows.name: Spotted Salamander
rows.interpretation: Look for the jelly surrounding an egg mass. Photograph the whole mass and its immediate setting without moving it.

rows.name: Clemens’ Agonopterix
rows.interpretation: A close photograph of a resting moth can preserve the wing markings needed for an identification. Add whether it was found at a light or away from one.

rows.name: yellow trout lily
rows.interpretation: Look at the mottling on the leaves as well as any flower. A photograph of the entire plant helps separate flowering from leaf-only records.

rows.name: northern starflower
rows.interpretation: Use the leaf arrangement and any visible bloom together. A second visit can show how much changed since the first photograph.

rows.name: Gray Treefrog
rows.interpretation: The linked dates show encounters. A sound recording with a timestamp would add direct evidence of calling.

rows.name: Common Baskettail
rows.interpretation: Look closely at the base of the hindwing when comparing the photograph with a field guide.

sources.label: New York State DEC on spring amphibian movements

bird_examples.name: Rusty Blackbird
bird_examples.note: This April checklist records Rusty Blackbird at Kingfisher Hollow on one visit.

summer.title: Summer at Kingfisher Hollow
summer.intro: Summer settles in around the pond and creek. Dragonflies hunt above the water by day, moths fly after dusk, and plants fill in the wet margins as the season advances.
summer.next_observation: Pick one pond vantage point and return to it on two summer dates. Spend the same amount of time watching, and record the weather, time, and what each animal was doing.

passages.title: The pond in daylight
passages.body: A dragonfly's life straddles the waterline. A mature nymph climbs out of the water and sheds its skin, then takes to the air to hunt once its wings harden.
passages.look_for: Record whether a dragonfly was perched, flying, or emerging. Photograph any shed skin in place and mark it as a separate kind of evidence.

claims.text: Eastern Pondhawks are among the dragonflies of midsummer at the Hollow.

passages.title: After dark
passages.body: Warm summer evenings extend insect activity beyond daylight. As dragonflies settle for the night, many moths take to the air around the woods and field edges.
passages.look_for: Use the same light and checking time for repeat visits. Record the hours and weather, even when there is little to photograph.

claims.text: The Lettered Habrosyne is among the moths active after dusk at the Hollow.

passages.title: The tangle at the creek edge
passages.body: By late summer, plants fill in the wet margins of the creek. Arrow-leaved tearthumb threads its stems through streamside growth, and vegetation in shallow water can offer cover for crayfish.
passages.look_for: Include a whole plant and a close view of its leaf shape. If you see a crayfish, photograph the animal where it is and include the streambed or bank in the frame.

rows.name: Eastern Pondhawk
rows.interpretation: Date and life stage answer different questions. Keep an adult sighting, a shed skin, and observed emergence as separate records.

rows.name: Pickerel Frog
rows.interpretation: A photograph of the back can preserve the shape and arrangement of the spots for identification.

rows.name: Lettered Habrosyne Moth
rows.interpretation: The pale bands on the wings are details to keep in focus. An observation time or light-check note adds context to the date.

rows.name: arrow-leaved tearthumb
rows.interpretation: Include where the pointed leaves join the stem. If you can see flowers or fruits, frame those separately so the stage can be recorded.

rows.name: Calico Crayfish
rows.interpretation: A view from above can show the outline of the body and claws. A wider view preserves context for the encounter.

autumn.title: Autumn at Kingfisher Hollow
autumn.intro: Goldenrods flower as the woods begin to change color. With leaf fall, fresh litter joins the wood already breaking down on the forest floor, and some insects stay active into November.
autumn.next_observation: Return to one woodland edge and one waterside spot in September, October, and November. Record the time and conditions at each stop and separate flowers, fungal fruiting bodies, and insect encounters in your notes.

passages.title: At the goldenrod edge
passages.body: Goldenrods flower along open edges while much of the canopy is still green. Their clusters of small yellow blooms supply pollen and nectar to insects into early autumn.
passages.look_for: Frame the stem, leaves, and flower heads together. Photograph any insect you see visiting a flower and write down what it was doing.

claims.text: At the Hollow, flowering goldenrod is a recurring sign of September.

passages.title: Look down to fallen wood
passages.body: As leaves fall, they add a fresh layer of litter over branches and logs already breaking down. Fungi help return nutrients from dead wood to the forest floor. Puffballs and bracket fungi are among the forms that fruit on wood.
passages.look_for: Record what a fungus is growing on and photograph the underside when you can see it without breaking anything off.

passages.title: Along the bank and after dark
passages.body: As autumn cools, mild days and evenings can still bring insect activity. Dragonflies and moths can both extend the season after many of the leaves are down.
passages.look_for: Note the time and conditions beside a dragonfly photograph. For a moth, add whether you found it at a light or away from one.

claims.text: At the Hollow, both Bicolored Sallows and Autumn Meadowhawks can still turn up in November.

rows.name: wrinkle-leaved goldenrod
rows.interpretation: Leaf texture and flower-head arrangement are worth capturing in the same view. The dates mark encounters, with flowering shown where it is documented.

rows.name: Pear-shaped Puffball
rows.interpretation: Use the photographs as identification leads. A view of the cluster and the material directly beneath it would help a reviewer.

rows.name: Conifer Mazegill
rows.interpretation: The underside and type of wood are details to document when checking this identification.

rows.name: Autumn Meadowhawk
rows.interpretation: The dates give a window of documented encounters. Close side views that show the legs and face can help check a meadowhawk identification.

rows.name: Bicolored Sallow
rows.interpretation: Open the records to compare the dates and wing patterns. Recording how each moth was found would make the timing easier to interpret.

winter.title: Winter at Kingfisher Hollow
winter.intro: Leaf fall opens the woods between the pond and creek. Some insects spend the cold months in shelter, while mammals that remain active leave tracks across the snow.
winter.next_observation: Repeat a short walk from the same starting point after fresh snow. Take a wide picture of any track trail and a close view with a scale, then record the snow conditions and time.

passages.title: Read the open woods
passages.body: When hardwoods lose their leaves, more light reaches the ground and the conifers stay green. Snow and ice can accent the difference between the broad surface of the pond and the creek winding past it.
passages.look_for: Frame the bank and water together from a safe position. Note how much snow or ice you can see from that spot.

passages.title: Check the sheltered edges
passages.body: Protected places carry some insects through winter. Adults of some species spend the cold months beneath loose bark or in sheltered cracks, ready to resume activity when conditions warm.
passages.look_for: Check sheltered surfaces without moving bark or disturbing leaf litter. If an insect is visible, photograph where it was resting as well as the insect.

claims.text: The Western Conifer Seed Bug is one of the insects that make it through winter as an adult.

passages.title: Follow the signs
passages.body: Some mammals keep moving through the woods all winter. Fishers are active through the cold months, and snow can preserve the tracks they leave as they travel.
passages.look_for: Photograph a run of prints before walking through it. Add a scale and note whether the snow is fresh, crusted, or melting.

rows.name: Western Conifer Seed Bug
rows.interpretation: Adults of this species can overwinter in sheltered places. A winter date records one encounter. A wider photograph can help show the kind of shelter where it was seen.

sources.label: US Forest Service field guide to Western Conifer Seed Bug

rows.name: American Mink
rows.interpretation: A camera image, track, and direct sighting are different kinds of evidence. Keep the method and date with the observation.

rows.name: Fisher
rows.interpretation: Look at the sequence and spacing of prints as well as individual toes when comparing a track trail with a guide. Multiple dated records can show repeat encounters even when the individuals cannot be told apart.

sources.label: New York State DEC on identifying Fisher signs

rows.name: Gray Fox
rows.interpretation: A camera image can be checked for visible features. Save the original frame so the whole animal and its posture are available for review.

bird_examples.name: Red Crossbill
bird_examples.note: This December checklist includes a photographed Red Crossbill at Kingfisher Hollow.
